utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you may continue your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Marinkovic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday we were discussing the question related to elections of judges, and we were dealing with paragraph 87 that had to do with the dismissal of Judges. I'm not going to ask you about all the rest, but I would like you to tell us more about this. Could you please tell us quite precisely whether you knew all the judges in the municipal district courts in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, were any Albanian judges dismissed from their jobs at the district and municipal courts in Pristina where you worked?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one was dismissed. But in relation to this, I would like to add an explanation to make things clear. A judge who's elected cannot be dismissed, simply cannot be dismissed or removed from his job. According to the law on judges, a judge's term may expire, or if he or she meets requests -- meets the requirements for retirement or if he or she asks for that himself or herself. Also, if a judge commits a crime that entails a six-month sentence at least, or if he does anything that makes him unfit to be a judge, or if proceedings are initiated because he does not carry out his duties as a judge conscientiously. So a judge cannot be removed from his job or dismissed any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Marinkovic. Since you mentioned all the legal terms and conditions under which a judge can be removed, of course I'm not going to deal with retirement, when one meets the requirements for retirement, but what is written here is that many judges were removed. Was a single judge removed?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not a single judge in this period that is mentioned in this paragraph, no. Neither before that nor after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you recall from that time, 1990, because paragraph 87 relates to 1990, do you remember all the judges who were on the district court, your colleagues? You said that from 1984, you were a judge on the district court in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember all the judges, because at that time in 1984, when I was elected to the district court in Pristina as a judge, many judges had already been working there. As for the ethnic make-up at the time, it was diverse. At that time in 1984 when I became a judge, there were more Albanian judges than the rest of us. I can say by way of an example that on the criminal chamber, there was one Serb judge and three Albanian judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell us, please, in the court in Pristina, as far as the district court is concerned, and the municipal court, after 1990 and 1991, say up to 1999, up to 2000, were there any Albanian judges?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did anybody have any problems in these courts because they were not a Serb? For example, you're a Macedonian.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any problem on account of the fact that you're a Macedonian, that you're not a Serb?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Neither I nor the Albanian judges. We had no problems whatsoever if we worked according to the law and if we were professional and conscientious in the discharge of our duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was anybody removed because they did not work according to the law or because they had some problems?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any cases in which somebody would have to be removed in accordance with the law?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Not a single case?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please bear in mind now that at the end of this paragraph some kind of abolition of a local court in Pristina is referred to. The only thing I can assume is that it was the Supreme Court of Kosovo that was abolished and that that is what was referred to, because no local courts were abolished. Or, rather, I'm going to ask you. Were any local courts in Pristina abolished?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But before I give this concrete answer, I should like to say that according to our law on the courts, there never was any such thing as a local court under that name. There were municipal courts, district courts, and the Supreme Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, let us say very precisely what it was that was abolished. After the constitution of 1990 was passed, there was only one Supreme Court in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, until then there was a Supreme Court of Kosovo and a Supreme Court of Vojvodina, and after the adoption of the constitution there is only one Supreme Court of Serbia. The district court and the municipal court in Pristina remained the same. Did the Supreme Court of Serbia have its own department in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Supreme Court of Serbia had its department in Pristina and another department of its own in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In charge of the respective areas of the provinces?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In this department of the Supreme Court in Pristina, were there any Albanians? As far as I can remember, there were three judges in that department of the Supreme Court in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In that department of the Supreme Court that was in charge of Kosovo and Metohija, there was one Albanian judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Out of a total of three judges?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was the total number in your district court?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our district court there was a total of 19 judges, together with the president of the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You knew all 19?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So none of them were removed?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please give us an explanation now lest there be any misunderstanding: Were there any cases of persons leaving their jobs of their own free will in order to open law offices of their own or to do some other job?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were such cases. Some colleagues asked for termination of their duties as judges by themselves, and then they became attorneys at law and they opened their own law offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, since in 1992 there was a general re-election of judges, did Albanian judges apply again for the post of judges? For example, in your district court, did they?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992 when there was general re-election of judges in the territory of all of Serbia, in our district judge [as interpreted] there were Albanians who also applied to the post of judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, let me ask the judge this: After the constitution of 1990 was passed, was there any change in the court system, any change at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were no changes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The courts that were there before the passing of the constitution remained afterwards.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that, Mr. Robinson, the witness bears in mind the fact that the constitution established only a single Supreme Court and that then the Supreme Courts of Kosovo and Vojvodina respectively became integral parts of the Supreme Court of Serbia and there were just departments in the two respective provinces dealing with the provinces themselves, but there were no other changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, now, you said that in the department of the Supreme Court of Serbia there was an Albanian judge. Were there any Albanian judges in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, the Albanian judge who was on that chamber went to Belgrade to be a judge on the Supreme Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And were there any Albanians who were judges in the Constitutional Court of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was an Albanian judge on the Constitutional Court of Belgrade -- of Serbia. I don't want to mention their names now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Their names are well known. That's no problem. It's a well-known fact who the judges of the Constitutional Court and the Supreme Court were.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have personal knowledge of the fact that there were such judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the Supreme Court and on the Constitutional Court.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, as an investigating judge, you conducted proceedings in several cases. Of course I'm not going to dwell on this entire period of your work, but you also conducted proceedings against terrorist groups in Kosovo and Metohija; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I would just like to acquaint the Trial Chamber with another thing; as for the status of an investigating judge. An investigating judge is not elected to that particular position. Annually, a schedule is made for the judges, and then one of the judges is appointed to be the investigating judge. So in 1994, according to this annual schedule which is adopted by the president of the court, and he makes it public at a joint session, for a particular year there is a schedule as to which judge is going to do what; who is going to deal with criminal cases, who is going to deal with civil cases, and who is going to be the investigating judge. That's the way we function until the present day. So there is no special capacity of investigating judge. Right now I work as a judge on the district court in Kragujevac and in the annual schedule for the year 2005, the president of the court appointed me to work on investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope that that is quite clear. Judges are elected without establishing previously who is going to do what, but then it is the president of the court who decides who is going to deal with criminal cases, who is going to deal with civil cases, who is going to be in charge of investigations, who is going to be in charge of litigations, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this additional explanation.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As an investigating judge in the district court in Pristina, I worked on a great many cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I asked you about these proceedings against terrorist groups in Kosovo and Metohija now. Tell me, was it only you or did the other judges on the district court of Pristina work on such cases?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I and other investigating judges in that period all worked on such cases. As regards terrorism, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Could you explain the principle according to which criminal cases - we're only talking about criminal cases now, irrespective of qualifications - how they were given to different investigating judges.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Criminal cases were dealt with by the court administration, and in accordance with the rules of procedure of the court, they were allocated to different judges according to a certain list, a certain order, irrespective of the person involved and irrespective of the parties involved and irrespective of the complexity of the legal matter involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: According to those legal provisions qualifies the crime, the charges brought against an individual.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The qualifications of a crime is done by the authorised public prosecutor and it is pursuant to his request or order that an investigation is undertaken against an individual if there is a well-founded suspicion that he has committed a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did you in your capacity of investigating judge receive your first case of that kind, that is a case involving terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received that first case at the end of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It means the same year that you were appointed investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that I was allocated and distributed as an investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, would you take a look at tab 1 now, please. And in tab 1 you will find an overview of cases in which you conducted the investigation as the investigating judge pursuant to a request by the prosecutor in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before I sit down, can I tell you the history of all these documents. The majority arrived late on Friday afternoon, some with, many without translations. The first index was provided, I think, on Monday night or Tuesday morning. No index of the documents on Friday. Further documents were provided yesterday. None of the documents, so far as we know, was listed on the 65 ter list, and thus far we haven't been able to connect these documents with any documents held in our own collection. It may be, as we saw with the last witness, that there can be an identity of documents with documents we held unknown to us. Thus this entire body of material comes to us in circumstances that we simply haven't been able to deal with it at all satisfactorily to date. I'm not going to seek to keep all the material out because I suspect that will be unrealistic and unhelpful, but I draw to the Court's attention the serious difficulties we are facing. As to tab 1, if it hasn't got a translation, there's nothing I can say about it at the moment because, although I do have language speakers available to me, they, like all other staff, are in short supply at the moment and it hasn't been possible to review the documents with the assistance of a language speaker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nice. Mr. Milosevic, there is a limit to the Court's tolerance and patience in relation to these many procedural irregularities. There's no translation for tab 1. How are we to proceed? It's a fairly long document. Normally we would place it on the ELMO if it were a short document, but it's fairly long. What is the explanation for these irregularities? Exhibits should have been mentioned long before and brought to the attention of the prosecutor and the Court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I take that on board fully, Mr. Robinson, and I do my best to make available the exhibits as soon as they come in my possession. However, with regard to the time that we had at our disposal, I was able to see Mrs. Marinkovic only last week. In this particular case, we are talking about the files that she managed to save when she had to leave Kosovo and Metohija. So they are just court files. They are not - how shall I put this? - any newspapers or information given in that way. They are just court files which she has safeguarded. She worked on many cases, and this is something that remains in her possession, because the archives are -- she doesn't have access to archives of the court in Pristina, if an archive still exists, unless it has been destroyed on the part of those who are exercising power and authority over there now. And what she managed to save is contained in this tab and these exhibits. What we provide in tab 1, the overview of cases, is for your assistance, to help you, because it says "Overview of cases in which Danica Marinkovic as the investigating judge conducted an investigation pursuant to a request from the public prosecutor --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- "of Pristina."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The management of your case is your responsibility, and you should not have brought the witness if you knew that the exhibits were not ready and in a form that they could be understood and available for consideration by the Court. We will have to consider how to deal with these exhibits. We will have to consider, quite frankly, whether to allow you to rely on them, because this is not the first or the second or the third time that something like this has happened.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Mr. Robinson, yes, I understand that fully, and that's quite in order, but I'll ask the witness this: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do individual files from these criminal cases that are contained in tab 1, are they just enumerated -- that are just enumerated, are they to be found in the tabs to follow as individual exhibits?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They are to be found in the following tabs.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now take a look, Mr. Robinson, at tab 2, for example. Tab 2 has been translated. Tab 2 is translated, so perhaps we could mark tab 1 for identification because the translation is ongoing in that case, and the idea was for us to use it as a document to help us out. But tab 2 is translated. It is an indictment which lists the perpetrators and how the proceedings were conducted. So you have that in translation. Most of the exhibits have been translated, and you do have them in your tabs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what we are talking about is not only the translation but also the disclosure to the Prosecution. So bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In any event, Mr. Milosevic, what is the purpose of tab 1, the chronology of cases in which the judge was involved, cases, what is it, in 1994? Why are you adducing that evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am adducing that evidence because I thought that that would be of assistance for you to be able to follow the documents to come, because it is an overview drafted and compiled by Judge Marinkovic on the basis of the documents which are described -- which describe these cases in detail. So the idea was that this should be of assistance, for a better understanding of the cases and the subject matter in hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think what would be helpful to us is her evidence in relation to the matter that she has come to testify about, which is, I think, Racak, 1999, not what happened in 1994. We've had a lot of background evidence. We don't need more background evidence, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is the first judge who has case files and proof and evidence, and we can see, looking at those cases, a great deal about terrorist activity, on the one hand, and parallel to that, the way in which the state reacted on the other through its legal means and the resources it had; uncovering the perpetrators, bringing the perpetrators to justice, bringing them to court, undertaking legal proceedings. All that is contained in those documents. So it is very essential, because this is the first time we have a judge who worked on these matters. Racak is one case in point. It was one investigation that Mrs. Marinkovic was engaged in. I selected a certain number of cases here which are -- illustrate how those cases were conducted during those years, during that period, because many things have been shown quite incorrectly here. So her testimony is essential to show what was done and what steps were taken in cases of that kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Evidence about terrorist activities per se by itself is not helpful. I mean, it will be helpful and relevant if it relates to one of the charges in the indictment. I have said this time and time again. If she has evidence from her work about terrorist activities that pertain to something in the indictment, then, yes, it will be relevant. Otherwise, it's not relevant. We are not -- we are not an academic institution here. We are not writing a history about terrorist activities. We have a specific indictment with specific charges. If tab 1 is just evidence about terrorist activities, totally unrelated to the allegations in the indictment, I will not allow it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, we notice that the tab has exhibits 1998, tab 14, which are closer to the events at hand. It would seem reasonable to allow the accused to concentrate on that period which is closer to the indictment period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. First of all, there are nine outstanding translations from the 65 tabs. It so happens that this is a full tab, tab 1, the first one we're looking at, and it is a summary of the witness's involvement in various cases over a period of, say, seven or eight years. There are earlier case reports which are within this bundle, but they demonstrate the issues that this witness as a judge was having to deal with in relation to activities within the province of Kosovo. In many respects, they go to show the course of her practice as a judge and that she was carrying out her duties in a particular way. From 1998, we, of course, get more proximate to issues within the indictment, but the earlier investigations demonstrate the kind of problems that she was dealing with as a judge in the region, and they're relevant for the issues that the accused has expounded as part of his defence concerning the issue of terrorism within Kosovo and the way that the state authorities were having to deal with it. In many respects, the accused will have anticipated that this witness will be under attack by the Prosecution because she was the judge who was involved in the investigation of the killings at Racak. So it's a legitimate exercise to say that he wishes to establish her bona fides, her professionalism, and do that by looking at her previous investigations. How much time is spent on that is another matter, and it would seem to me that there could be a rapid run-through setting up the witness in relation to those earlier investigations before getting to the more substantial investigations which are proximate to the indictment, which, as the Trial Chamber has observed, is from tab 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Kay. That's helpful. Mr. Nice, just on the question of the relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know if I can help with a couple of observations. First of all it may be helpful to know how much of what Mr. Kay said is in fact adopted by the accused. Second, I don't know if you have the 65 ter summary to hand. If you haven't, can I read what it says? It says: "Judge in Pristina; Racak; all events in Kosovo and Metohija;" and then it goes on to say: "personal knowledge of the activities of the parties to the conflict during the war in Kosovo, personal knowledge of the parties to the conflict of Racak undertook the investigation of the Racak case." So apart from the single phrase "all events in Kosovo and Metohija," which might be ambiguous, the 65 ter summary forecasts evidence strictly limited to Racak. As to these files or any of them that relate to a period before Racak, there may be issues as to whether they're admissible at all, and if so, for what purpose, because I'm not sure whether the accused will be relying on them for the same limited purpose that Mr. Kay volunteered. If the accused wants them to be admitted for a wider purpose, for example, to show the truth of the underlying allegations made or found by the legal authorities concerned, that may create difficulties. It may create legal difficulties - we'll have to address those if and when the application to produce the documents is concerned - and it may create factual difficulties if I discover, on investigations that I'm able to make, that there are views that these trials were other than by due process and by fair process. So there are a number of problems. My initial position would be to invite the Chamber to restrict the witness to the material forecast in the 65 ter summary, which would be Racak and simply Racak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I will read to you the paragraph 93 - I'm not going to ask the witness about it - since you say that it has to be related to the indictment in order for me to ask questions, but I also believe it has to be related to previous testimony, et cetera. But look at paragraph 93: "While the wars were being conducted in Slovenia, Croatia, and Bosnia-Herzegovina, the situation in Kosovo, while tense, did not erupt into the violence and intense fighting seen in the other countries. In the mid-1990s, however, a faction of the Kosovo Albanians organised a group known as UCK, or known in English as the Kosovo Liberation Army. This group advocated a campaign of armed insurgency and violent resistance to the Serbian authorities. In mid-1996, the KLA began launching attacks, primarily targeting Serbian police forces. Thereafter, and throughout 1997, Serbian police forces responded with forceful operations against suspected KLA bases and supporters in Kosovo." Thus I have read out to you the entire paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Milosevic. We'll allow you to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice -- Mr. Nice, you can see how that immediately raises a problem for the Bench, unless of course you were to withdraw that allegation because it may be thought by you to be irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes. And that's a different issue, if I may say so, from whether this witness can give this evidence now. I'm -- I find myself in this rather difficult position with the accused taking us by surprise with the material that he presents us, because on the one hand I have no desire to stop his laying -- no desire at all to stop him presenting you with material that is helpful and relevant. On the other hand, I need to be able to deal with it in a satisfactory way, and there's the problem. Now, if this witness can help with the paragraph that the accused read out, and if the Court is minded to overlook its own requirements of compliance with Rule 65 ter, something that it referred to recently, saying that it was going, I think, to limit the accused to 65 ter, then the next process -- the next step in the dealings with this witness will be to assess when and how I'm in a position to cross-examine on whatever she says. It happens -- and I don't say this to encourage any particular easing of its own restrictions, it happens that the witness's evidence is forecast to last nine hours, which would take us until the end of tomorrow, and that there is then a ten-day gap over which many people might be expecting to have holidays or otherwise to be away from the seat of the Tribunal. Nevertheless, there may be the possibility of using that time to some advantage, and it's my purpose here to do the best I can to assist the Chamber. This, incidentally, is without prejudice to arguments that may have to be raised and I may raise almost immediately about the admissibility of the documents themselves, but that comes next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the Chamber is bending over to be fair to you and to be lenient. The Chamber, of course, also has to bear in mind the Rules under which the Tribunal operates. None of these exhibits has been listed in your exhibit list, so that technically you should not be allowed to rely on them at all. We are going to allow you, but you have to move very quickly. There is no need to spend a lot of time on these matters which pre-date 1998. We will allow you to refer to the exhibits. Those that are not translated we will mark for identification. But we are now going to warn you that the next time that this happens, we will not allow you to rely on exhibits that have not been placed on your exhibit list. This is happening all too frequently, and it makes the work of the Chamber that much more difficult. But bear in mind you have to move quickly through these matters leading up to 1998. The principal purpose of this witness's testimony is to hear her evidence on Racak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that is your opinion, and I have nothing against your opinion, but it is the purpose of this witness to talk about other relevant things as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But you should have said that in your 65 ter. That's Mr. Nice's point. You're on very weak ground there, so don't press that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson. Mr. Robinson, what you are saying is true, and I have no quarrel with that. I didn't say that under 65 ter, indeed, but I had no time to say it because of the time you allowed me. I had no chance to contact this witness prior to this hearing to establish what evidence she is able to provide. And I have to remind you that in -- during the presentation of the Prosecution case, I received entire binders to review, and I was always told that I had enough time overnight to review the material. So it is not at all true that the other side complied with some strict rule of prior disclosure. You remember well, Mr. Robinson, as does Mr. Kwon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I remember very well, and that's one of the reasons why we are being fairly lenient, yes. So proceed on the basis that I have identified.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, D290 will be given to these two binders of documents. Tab 1 will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, you participated as the investigating judge in a large number of cases. Was that the result of your -- of some privileged status of yours in the district court in Pristina or did you simply have a large number of cases?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We simply had a large number of cases, including criminal reports and requests for investigations, so that our experience with that affected the way we proceeded in those cases, not only in my case but it was the case of other judges as well, in Pristina as well as throughout Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the relevant time did the Criminal Code of Yugoslavia include the crime of terrorism?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the Criminal Code of Yugoslavia, Article 125 stipulates the crime of terrorism.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was it like?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to remind everyone that the Criminal Code of Yugoslavia is already in evidence, has been since the Prosecution case, which is why I did not provide it as a separate exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How is it defined in Article 125, the crime of terrorism?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I shall read to you from Article 125 of the Criminal Code of Yugoslavia adopted and enacted in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and it was applied throughout the territory of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, you're being asked by the interpreters to speak more slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we have it on the ELMO, please, interpreters request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, would the usher please place it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Any person who causes an explosion or a fire or undertakes another action causing a general danger or an act of violence creating a feeling of unsafety among the citizenry in the intent of jeopardising the constitutional order and security of the SFRY shall be sentenced to at least three years."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, very well. What, to the best of your knowledge, was the purpose of the KLA and other similar organisations created in Kosovo at the time while you were investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The principal purpose of the terrorist organisation which called itself the KLA was forcible secession from Yugoslavia, creation of a separate date or annexation to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us be as brief as possible. Did the Criminal Code of Yugoslavia include a crime -- a stipulation whose purpose was to protect the territorial integrity?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was Article 116. That regulated crimes against territorial units and integrity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We shall not read it. In this paragraph 93 that I quoted a moment ago, of the Kosovo indictment, it says: "... a faction of Kosovo Albanians organised a group ... which pursued a campaign of armed insurgence and violent resistance to Serbian authorities." Did the Yugoslav criminal law envisage a crime relating to such an organisation or association?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Criminal Code envisaged the crime of jeopardising territorial integrity envisaged under Article 106.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Association for hostile -- for the purpose of engaging in hostile activities, was that also envisaged?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Article 116, which envisaged crimes against territorial integrity, and 106, association for purposes of engaging in hostile activities. You mentioned also the article relating to terrorism. Correction, 125. You mentioned those three articles of the Criminal Code. Was association for purposes of hostile activities regulated in general terms?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. In the Criminal Code of Yugoslavia in chapter 15 there is a list of crimes against the constitutional order and security of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Since you quoted or invoked several of these legal provisions pursuant to which you acted as investigating judge when conducting such cases, I shall ask you, did you in your experience as investigating judge in cases involving the KLA, did you apply all three of these provisions of the law? We are talking now about jeopardising of territorial integrity, terrorism, and association for the purpose of engaging in hostile activities.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were all those grounds taken into account in the cases you conducted?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In investigations where I acted as investigating judge pursuant to the request of the district prosecutor of Pristina, the accused were charged with all three crimes; the crime of association for the purpose of hostile activities, the crime of terrorism, and the crime of jeopardising territorial integrity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, there was association for the purpose of engaging in hostile activity and the aim of that activity was to jeopardise the territorial entity and the vehicle was terrorism.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, what about the organisation of Albanian separatists? I'm just talking about separatists now. Organisation into illegal para-statal organisations. Did you take part in any such proceedings?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This kind of illegal association was not investigated. I did not have such cases and I did not conduct such investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did our organs tolerate those forms of para-statal organisation that did not take an armed form? For example, parallel illegal schooling, health care, as they called it, parallel? Was any action taken against such activities?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The state did not bring any charges in respect of such activities. This was tolerated. The parallel schools and the parallel health institutions were operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As a judge, do you know -- could you give me an unequivocal answer as to whether any criminal proceedings were conducted because of that.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No proceedings were conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about the illegal organisation of some para-statal forms, if I can put it that way, that implied arming or espionage or similar activities was prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was criminal prosecution in such cases by the relevant state authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now I'm going to go back to paragraph 93. I'm not going to read all of it, as I didn't a minute ago, but I would just like to draw your attention to some parts. It says in the mid-1990s the KLA was established, and then it says: "In mid-1996, it began launching attacks primarily targeting Serbian police forces." And then "Thereafter, and throughout 1997, police forces, Serbian police forces responded with forceful operations..." Do you have any particular knowledge about the inception and activities of the KLA and other terrorist organisations in Kosovo and Metohija and what it says here in the mid-1990s? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I worked as an investigating judge and when I dealt with the kind of criminal cases that I mentioned a few minutes ago, I became aware that a terrorist organisation that called itself the KLA was established in the beginning of 1992, and before that they started preparations and organisational activities to that end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's pause here for a moment. According to your knowledge, it was in 1992. So what it says here in the mid-1990s is not correct. On the basis of what are you saying this?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am saying this on the basis of the investigations that I carried out in a large number of cases where the suspects were Albanians, and when they gave statements to me as an investigating judge, they talked about all of this. What they said was corroborated by a great deal of evidence. And on the basis of these comprehensive investigations, we established these facts that were relevant for the prosecution so that the prosecutor could continue such proceedings by bringing an indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Are you talking about -- or, rather, now we are establishing the accuracy of what the indictment says from several different aspects. When you say that as investigating judge in Pristina you had investigations against several persons and that through these investigations you came to this information, do you bear in mind a court document which was provided in tab 2 here? It's --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gentlemen, you have a translation of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says "Republic of Serbia, Autonomous Province of Kosovo and Metohija, District Public Prosecutor's Office," and then -- I hope that you have received a list of the tabs. I would like to draw your attention to this. Please take a look at it and then give us appropriate explanations. On page 2 -- or, rather, on page 3, it says: "Because." That's the rationale: "From mid-1992 to early 1997, they formed an enemy terrorist association called the 'Kosovo Liberation Army,' which operated throughout the area ..." et cetera, et cetera. So I am going to skip part of this paragraph, and then towards the very end of this paragraph in the rationale --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Milosevic, you must ensure that everybody has found the passage to which you're referring before you move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Page 4 in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Page 4.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have page 4 in the English language. It says: "[In English] Because. From mid-1992 to early 1997, they formed an enemy terrorist association called 'Kosovo Liberation Army...'" et cetera. [Interpretation] I've already quoted that part. Then it says what they did. All of it is in that same paragraph. And they obtained "a large quantity of weapons: Automatic rifles, sniper rifles, pistols, ammunition, hand grenades, various explosive devices, rifle grenades and other explosives; and they conducted dozens of attacks on Ministry of the Interior members and buildings, buildings where refugees were sheltered, and buildings for such persons that were still under construction, buildings where Serbs and Montenegrins gathered, and attacked a number of Serbian, Montenegrin, and Albanian citizens --" that is to say Serbs, Montenegrins, and Albanians "-- whereby they intentionally killed or attempted to kill a number of persons in various ways." And it also says that they issued 29 statements in which they claimed responsibility for these terrorist attacks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the question now, Mr. Milosevic, having read that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question was when Mrs. Marinkovic gave an answer stating that they were established in 1992 and when it says here in mid-1990s, she said it was not correct, and I asked her on the basis of what you are claiming that, and then she said that she's claiming that on the basis of the fact that she conducted an investigation against several persons. Then I took this tab in order to read out whether these were some elementary assertions, whether the file itself shows that what you are saying is correct, the court file, the case file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We proceed on basis of question and answer, Mr. Milosevic. You are not giving evidence. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the witness answers, I delayed questioning the admissibility of this tab until I saw where the accused was taking us. And the fact that the conclusions drawn may - I simply don't know at the moment - may be conclusions that the Prosecution would accept because, of course, the Prosecution accepts the KLA was a developing body doing things in the 1990s, doesn't mean we should overlook any procedural problems that should properly be considered before this document is exhibited. It appears that the accused wants the document to be admitted in some way for the truth of what it sets out. Here is the problem: There is, I think, no jurisprudence, at least, I haven't turned up any so far, though I've only just come to grips with what the accused wishes to prove through these tabs, there is no jurisprudence dealing specifically with how the records of another court should be dealt with in this court, and that might be quite a tricky problem given that allegations are made about the fairness and particular unfairness of proceedings in the various courts of the former Yugoslavia. Second, to what degree is the work of a judge dealing with people speaking to her or making statements that she reads different from the proposed evidence of the investigator Barney Kelly covering Kosovo, which was rejected by the Trial Chamber, rejection that was confirmed as appropriate by the Appeals Chamber. I have the Appeals Chamber decision here. I'm sure you're familiar with. I can refer you to it, if necessary, but it will take time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, can Barney Kelly's statements be compared with a court record?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I go back: There is no particular jurisprudence that says, as far as I'm aware, that gives a special status to the work of judges or courts in the courts of the former Yugoslavia or investigative judges and their findings. Their work is similar in format and category to that of an investigator who reviews an amount of material and draws conclusions. And it was the conclusions in particular that were rejected, both by the Chamber and by the Appeals Chamber, and even by His Honour Judge Shahabuddeen, the Presiding Judge of the Chamber, who expressed a partially dissenting decision. So here's the problem with this tab and this witness: One, had the material been served in advance and had it been possible for me to consider it in detail, it might be that I would have admitted it and proposed admission as a way of using the court process to save time, something the accused knows we are prepared to do but hasn't invited us to engage in. Two, this particular exhibit would appear, on the jurisprudence of this Chamber and the Appeals Chamber, to be prima facie inadmissible if its adduction is not for the limited purpose that Mr. Kay identified earlier, namely what issues did the witness have to deal with but for the purpose of the truth of what it says. Your Honours, those are my submissions in brief. I would respectfully remind you that part of the Appeals Chamber's decision in rejecting the summarising witness proposal of the Prosecution was that cross-examining the person who summarises the statement or who would draw conclusions that -- who summarises the statement doesn't overcome the absence of the opportunity to cross-examine the persons who made them. So that in a case like this were it to be the case, and I simply don't know, that I would wish to challenge the underlying evidence, the fact that I have an opportunity to cross-examine this witness doesn't save the document from being prima facie inadmissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Nice, what you're saying is that the documents relating to Racak is not admissible either.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We haven't reached that yet. If you mean the documents of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because, of course, I know and I'm sure the Court remembers, that she conducted an on-site investigation so that she will be giving, or to some degree she will be giving evidence of things that she saw and did herself. That's rather different. Here, as far as I can understand it, she's operating as, I think it's going to be an investigative judge, taking evidence in one form or another, summarising it, and expressing opinions on it, both of which were rejected by this Chamber and by the Appeals Chamber, and in broadly parallel circumstances. So if I may respectfully say so, Racak comes later, but looking at this material -- and I'm not taking a technical point unhelpfully because I've indicated if the material is something I'd admit, I'd admit it, but I haven't been given a chance to check it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Summarised contemporaneously at that time, not for the purpose of this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does that make any difference in the circumstances? I respectfully suggest no. Just one -- Mr. Saxon helpfully reminds me that that issue was also specifically set aside as of relevance by the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your objection here, though, Mr. Nice, isn't to the document because you acknowledge that it does have certain probative value as characterised by Mr. Kay. Your objection is to the questions that are going to be asked, which is rather different, I think, although the argument's the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. What --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I can see no problem with the document itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The document itself might be simply be unnecessary because if the witness simply says in the course of so many years I had to deal with certain issues of the following types, do you need a document to prove it unless it's challenged? These documents are plainly being introduced for the truth of conclusions drawn, conclusions that I'm not in a position to accept at the moment and therefore I have to invite the Chamber to deal carefully with an admission of a document that, admitted now in this form, might then operate as a precedent for admitting a document of the same category at a later stage when its contents would be completely challenged by the Prosecution. As it is, and the Chamber will understand this, if we're going to have several of these documents to look at, this first one I think has something like 21 named defendants or accused, and the Chamber can well understand that there are very grave difficulties facing anybody who wishes to check the acceptability of the conclusions drawn in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we don't get the conclusions here, do we?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think the passage that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: They're recommendations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not sure what the cause amounts to and that's why I waited to hear what it was that the accused was going to ask the witness before raising to discuss with you the admissibility of this as a document. It appears it's a document that comes from somebody else, if we look at page 26.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's the prosecutor. Well, the whole document needs to be explained to us a little bit more. Your Honour, I've taken enough time to set out my position and I can't help any further unless you have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is nothing like the Barney Kelly example at all. The Prosecution seems to be putting forward a series of arguments over the last few months and weeks to make out that they've been disadvantaged in some way and that the accused is getting a much fairer trial than they are. It's not actually them that's on trial, and that's certainly not the case. Barney Kelly was an investigator for the Prosecution who summarised a large number of witness statements after the events and that was put forward as evidence by the Prosecution and rejected by the Trial Chamber. These are contemporaneous documents. They're public records. They're in no way dissimilar to other documents put forward by the Prosecutor during its case when it put forward public documents as matters and containing information that were relevant to the time, and that's exactly what these documents do. Mr. Nice should be concentrating on his indictment rather than on the issues that he's raising concerning these documents and dealing with ways of putting his case as a means of proving his indictment rather than contesting these issues. It's the accused's Defence that he wants this information in to show the workings of this witness as a judge. As far as the indictment is concerned and the Prosecutor, that might not be relevant to them although it is relevant to the accused's Defence. In our submission, this is plainly admissible evidence. It is probative, it is relevant, and it doesn't in any way breach the jurisprudence of this Tribunal. This is not the first time that a matter like this has been discussed. These are public documents that are capable of being considered by this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, perhaps you could tell us how -- how you work. When you collect your statements, you interview witnesses, and do you then draw certain conclusions, and what happens to those conclusions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just inform you. As an investigating judge, when I act upon the request of the authorised public prosecutor and get the go-ahead for conducting an investigation against individuals, as an investigating judge I collect proof and evidence and information that is vital so that at the end of the investigation the prosecutor can access -- assess whether he's going to raise an indictment or abandon the investigation further. All the suspects are interviewed. I talk to them pursuant to the code on criminal -- Criminal Code. When I read him his rights, the right Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to his defence, the right to the use of language, when I read out to him what he is being charged, when I read out the indictment and the crime, the description of the crime, through an interview with him he tells me about the charges brought against him. That's what I do with all suspects. After that, once I bring in a decision on going ahead with an investigation, I continue to collect proof and evidence during the investigative process which have been proposed by the public prosecutor. When I amass and combine all that information and those facts, then I send the matter back to the prosecutor who then -- if I find good cause, then I send the whole case back to the prosecutor and then he decides whether to raise an indictment or not. Once the indictment is raised, we go to trial and the main hearing is conducted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. So you make a determination as to whether there is good cause, do you, on the basis of the information that you have gathered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. After interviewing the suspects, I make -- bring in a decision to continue investigations, to uncover evidence and material. Before I reach that decision I cannot carry on with the legal proceedings and the investigation, and that is pursuant to the Criminal Code and Law on Criminal Procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, it has been said in some quarters that the Tribunal might benefit from the system of an investigating judge, but that's another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, but that would be an investigating judge of this court. And although I have not -- I'm not in a position yet to forecast - even to anticipate - what my line of cross-examination will be, it would be naive of us all not to recognise that there are allegations made one way and another in respect of the conduct of courts in the former Yugoslavia. And I come back to my earlier observation about there being no jurisprudence, no regulatory basis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There is jurisprudence. It's Rule 89(C).

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Dealing specifically with the findings of another court. And I make that observation because in some systems there is, and when the earlier finding of another court of the same court that's dealing with the matter is allowed into evidence, it's usually allowed into evidence with procedural limitations, sometimes, and with limitations as to the basis upon which it's allowed in. And it's clear that what would happen if this evidence goes in is that this witness will be allowed to give expressions of her opinion based on her investigations and/or -- and/or, if I may conclude, that the prosecutor himself will be allowed his opinions will stand. So those are the issues I raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, let's move on. We rule that it is admissible. Let us move on quickly.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to say one thing for the record. I think it is quite unacceptable what Mr. Nice is doing in comparing an investigator with an elected judge of a high court who is in court here to testify and who is bringing us official documents and not her impressions or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we have already dealt with the matter. Let us move --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They are public records, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, this tab is in fact an indictment against these individuals. Did you conduct the investigation in this particular case?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you conduct the investigation with all these individuals?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the basis your investigations, did the public prosecutor raise an indictment?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago when you explained to us how you conduct your investigation, how you interview the suspects, et cetera, do you talk to them alone, to the suspects alone?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who else is present?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I interview a suspect, we have the deputy public prosecutor present who tendered the request for the investigation, as well as his defence counsel and an interpreter, because in most cases --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. An interpreter is present when we're talking about somebody who is Albanian or Turkish or whatever; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But it's not simultaneous interpretation. It's consecutive. The interpreter translates my questions and then the answers, so the process is a little slower, which required quite a lot of time. We had to work out of hours in the afternoon and on weekends as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, let's leave that aside for the moment whether you worked after hours and put in extra hours or not. Let's clarify one matter. In the cases you have here listed here, when you conducted an investigation, was the prosecutor present? You said that actually it was the deputy prosecutor. Mr. Nice is a deputy prosecutor, he's not the Prosecutor, but anyway prosecutor, let's say. So you have the prosecutor present, you have a lawyer present, the defence counsel for the suspect; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the clerk taking the minutes, and an interpreter; right?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So all the interviews are conducted and all the statements are taken in the presence of those individuals; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then the minutes are taken, and on the basis of those records you make your conclusions and send the case back to the public prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not as an investigating judge myself make any conclusions of my own. I just collect the facts and the evidence, and then I send that material to the prosecutor and it is up to him to decide whether to go forward or not. In this particular case, according to this particular indictment, he did raise an indictment because he considered there was good cause and sufficient grounds to raise an indictment. And after that, we come to a ruling of the first instance court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, just a point of clarification: Not all of the suspects in this indictment had been detained. Some were at large.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of the 21 persons, three were at large. When I conducted my investigation, we did not -- the law enforcement organs were not -- did not have access to them. They couldn't find them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Simple question: You obviously were not able to interview them. Nevertheless, was an indictment prepared by the prosecutor against them even though they had not been interviewed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because the other suspects whom I did interview mentioned those individuals and talked about their activities, and this was later confirmed on the basis of the evidence that was collected during the investigation. And of the proof and evidence we found a large number of weapons, for example, and the authorities, on the basis of my order, searched the flats of these individuals and all the weapons listed here was found during that search in their apartments, and there is also evidence of this -- these weapons having been confiscated for them. They were in unlawful possession of weapons and weapons that were supposedly used during the terrorist acts they committed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic, we will have to take the break now. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, please continue. Remember, we want to move quickly over these areas leading up to 1998.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, I'd like to draw your attention to the fact that this is not provided just to show you what an investigating judge of the district court in Pristina, in this case Witness Danica Marinkovic did, but it illustrates the facts that were established and taken note of in public records which have been provided here as exhibits. So if it says in the indictment in the mid-1990s a faction set up by the KLA, and here in a public document, in public records we see that happened in 1992, as early as that, that means that is being challenged, just like many other facts. And I shall, of course, bear in mind your instructions and guidelines with respect to the documents, but I'd like to ask you to do the same and to understand that I was not given access to or did not have disposal of any archives. My associates only received the go-ahead 15 days ago to access certain documents from the Ministry of the Interior, for example, and their archives, and they had sought to be given that right for the past two or three years. I don't even have my own archive at my disposal, which is quite different from Mr. Nice's situation who has all the archives of this world at his disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, let's take note of one fact. You explained it to us a moment ago, but I'd like to take note of it now. An investigating judge in the proceedings that you explained during the investigation process does not bring in a single conclusion himself but just amasses evidence and grounds to show good cause. Is that the subject of what -- is that the gist of what you were saying?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. On this document, and we're talking about tab 2, which has been translated, I'd like to draw your attention to, gentlemen, the Serbian text of the document where there are handwritten notes which are not translated in the English version. They weren't taken into account, the handwritten portions. You can take a look at the Serbian text just to see what I mean. Figures and dates are written in in handwriting next to the names. Otherwise, the names as they are in the English text are written out, typed out in the Latin script. Now, Mrs. Marinkovic, whose hand notes are those? Who introduced those handwritten notes into the document? I'm talking about tab 2.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The handwritten notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says, for example, 20 years, et cetera, the figures.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was written by the district public prosecutor on his copy of the indictment, and I have to say in this regard that the indictment was raised by the district public prosecutor in Pristina, and the number is 25/97. It is the 25th of July, 1997 is the date. And it incorporates 21 individuals accused, three of which were at large, fugitives. However, there were two more individuals in this indictment. They were officers of the Albanian army who acted with this group and engaged in terrorist activities in Kosovo and Metohija but under pseudonyms. The pseudonym was Zoki and Zeni. Those two pseudonyms. Since their identity has not been established or was not established, they could not have been incorporated by this indictment. After the indictment was raised, however, and the legal proceedings and trial went ahead by the district court in Pristina, there was a verdict. They were found -- they had a judgement, and it is numbered 68/97 of the 16th of December, 1997, and that judgement, that verdict I did not have at my disposal, but on the basis of the judgement, they were found guilty. The individuals stated and set out here in the indictment were found guilty of having committed crimes, the crime of terrorism, pursuant to Article 125 of the Criminal Code of Yugoslavia. And pursuant to Article 139, para 2 of that same law we have the crime of association for the purpose of engaging in hostile activities. And Article 136 of the -- paragraph 1 of the Criminal Code. Of these 21 individuals, two persons were freed and found not guilty because there wasn't sufficient proof and evidence to find them guilty of the charges against them. The other individuals received prison sentences. They were found guilty. And the prison sentences are written down in handwriting next to each name. For example, Nait Hasani, the first accused, got a prison sentence of 20 years. Agron Toljaj also received a prison term of 20 years. Arif Voksi, once again 20 years' imprisonment. Hasan Zenelji got 15 years' imprisonment; Cerim Keljmendi, 15 years' imprisonment; Adrijan Krasnici, he was not sentenced because during the trial, as it says here next to his name, it says that he died. Aljban Neziri was set free. Agim Makoli received an 11 years' prison sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. You don't have to go through all the sentences. The public prosecutor then wrote in the results of the trial and his indictment in his own hand, using the judgement and verdict of the court; is that right? Is that what you were saying?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, gentlemen, I am not showing here or proving that they perpetrated terrorist attacks, killings, and so on and so forth. That was established by the court itself. The court reached that verdict. But these court files I am tendering as an exhibit showing that it occurred and that it occurred as of 1992, according to this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, apart from what we just established regarding year 1992, which says -- which is said in the indictment to be mid-1990s, in paragraph 93 it says that the KLA organised attacks primarily targeting Serbian police forces. Would you please tell me, according to the number of victims of these attacks perpetrated by the KLA, did those attacks target primarily civilians or police forces?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The attacks of the KLA terrorist organisation targeted mainly civilians; Serbs, Albanians, and all the others living in Kosovo and Metohija, as well as members of the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So when it says "targeting primarily Serbian police forces --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just to be clear about one thing, is it fair to say that every one of the specific allegations in the indictment relates to either late 1995 or to 1996 or 1997?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Reference to the judgement, to the terrorist acts perpetrated by this group relates to 1996. However, before that time they worked to organise and create an association or, rather, a gang which later grew into the terrorist organisation known as the KLA. I can read out to you very briefly the part that regards the first accused. It says: "In 1992, ending with 1995, together with the other accused, after meetings and agreements by procuring, transporting, and concealing materiel and weapons --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My question was simply related to the specific acts that they were said to have committed, and you've confirmed what I thought was the position. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Prior to that time, they prepared, they organised themselves, procured unlawful weapons as well as funds from abroad. They also procured funds through crime activities, organised crime, and the perpetration of criminal offences, not only in Kosovo and Metohija but in all of Europe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, in paragraph 93, after this sentence which says: "... primarily targeting the police forces of Serbia," a matter which we clarified a moment ago, a sentence follows that reads: "Thereafter, and throughout 1997 --" which means beginning with mid-1996 and throughout 1997 -- "Serbian police forces responded with forceful operations against suspected KLA bases and supporters in Kosovo." I would like to ask you, in 1996 and until the end of 1997, were there any forceful police operations at all, or did the police just react to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- to actions by investigating crimes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The latter part is leading. You have to ask her generally what was the reaction, if any, of the Serb police force.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am asking the witness questions related to paragraph 93, which says that in mid-1997 and "throughout 1997, Serbian police forces responded with forceful operations." That is a quotation from the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... to ask her, if she can answer it, what was the reaction of the police force. But you're asking her, Were there any forceful police operations at all or did the police just react to? and then I stopped you because that was leading.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, beginning with mid-1997 and throughout 1997, as it reads in the indictment, what was the reaction of the police force?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police did not react forcefully. The police did not use any violent means against the KLA. They only worked to identify perpetrators of crimes. There were no clashes, conflicts between the police and the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, were you at -- were you in the position to answer that question at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am in a position, because I spent a lot of my time working on investigations against a large number of suspects involved in these crimes, and through this work I acquired a lot of knowledge related to that matter, and I am presenting to you all the work that I did through which I witnessed all of these things in Kosovo and Metohija. And I claim that in the period mentioned there were no forceful police operations against the KLA. And if you look through the cases I conducted, you will see that. We will come to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that you can say that you were not involved in any case in which there was evidence of that, but how can you go beyond that? I mean, I would never dream of making a claim that -- about the whole jurisdiction of all the judges of the whole of Kosovo, that they had never encountered any example of Serb aggression. How can you possibly do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know, I claim because I know. I was an eyewitness, and I conducted thousands of upon thousands of on-site investigations in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You can speak about the cases in which you were an eyewitness but you've given a much wider answer than that that covers every set of circumstances in Serbia -- not just Kosovo; in Serbia, as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I am not saying anything of the kind. I'm talking only about the territory where I was authorised and competent to conduct investigations and on-site investigations. That is the area of Pristina, which is a smaller territorial unit, the district court of Pristina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please bear in mind one thing that can be proven with any number of witnesses and documents: The first police operation you could call a forceful operation happened in 1998 and it targeted the terrorist group of Adem Jashari.
