It was presented at the very beginning, when you were not here yet, but I see that it was omitted from the indictment because it turned out after all not to have been a crime and it turned out that it cannot be treated like a crime because the person involved was a murderer whom the police sought to arrest and who had previously been convicted to 20 years in prison, together with his group. So the first operation of that kind took place in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Judge Marinkovic, when this incident in Prekaze happen?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With regard to this reference of Adem Jashari, he was part of the group against which I conducted an investigation. The suspects were charged with the crime of terrorism. He was one of the suspects. After that, he became one of the convicts because he was a fugitive at the time of the investigation and inaccessible to the state authorities during the proceedings, during the trial. He was tried in absentia and convicted on two charges of terrorism involving crimes that caused the death of two policemen and civilians in Glogovac in Serbia, and Prekaz and Srbica. He was sentenced to 20 years in prison and an all-points alert was issued against him. So the law enforcement authorities continued to search for him based on both the indictment, which was confirmed, and the final judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the incident of -- in Prekaze when the group of Adem Jashari was liquidated?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. That was in March 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Stop there. Before March 1998, were there any similar police operations involving the surrounding or liquidation of a terrorist group?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there had been no such action before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in 1996 and 1997, there was nothing of the kind. Only in 1998 the group of Adem Jashari, who was already previously sentenced to 20 years in prison, was surrounded and killed by the police in Prekaze. Was that the first action?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does the witness confirm that that's what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. That's the way it happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You would describe that as forceful action by the Serb police to liquidate personnel suspected of being connected with a terrorist organisation. That's the way Mr. Milosevic characterises it. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, no. I did not qualify that as a forceful action. I qualified it as the first action of the police force aimed at arresting Jashari. Jashari being a person who was asked to surrender when surrounded, upon which he and his group kept firing at the police throughout that time. He was given several hours to surrender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You yourself, if you look back at the transcript, described the conduct as liquidating the group that was with Jashari. Are you departing from that description?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am saying that it was not an action aimed at liquidating the group. It was aimed at arresting Jashari; however, during the operation to arrest him, he was eventually liquidated, together with his group, because they had shot at the police all the time. The operation was originally intended to arrest them, just as all the others who were tried had been arrested by normal procedure. But unlike Jashari, they did not shoot at the police, and it was possible to arrest them. Jashari and the others were also meant to be arrested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What this demonstrates, may I suggest, Mr. Milosevic, is that it does not help to ask leading questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought it was not a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you know anything about the period immediately before the police attempt to arrest Adem Jashari in Donje Prekaze village? What was the situation in Donje Prekaze and the surrounding area?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, for many years before that the police had no access to Donje Prekaze because it held a large group of terrorists which kept walking about the place armed. So nobody dared access the village or come in. They also installed checkpoints and guards around the village so the police was unable for years to come into the village and go about their regular work, inspecting and patrolling the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know whether it's worth checking at this stage, whether this is in the area that the witness said was an area she could speak about or was outside it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm allowing you to proceed, but you must move quickly over these areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you deal with the question the Prosecutor raises. Is this within the area that you were responsible for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was, because the next group which I investigated on charges of terrorism included all the members of the terrorist group which was active in Donje Prekaze village, including Adem Jashari.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was Donje Prekaz village within your area of investigation, the area that your court covered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will tell you now: Donje Prekaze village is covered by the district court of Kosovska Mitrovica. However, since the group of terrorists that had been apprehended and suspected of having perpetrated a large number of crimes, including an attack on the police in Glogovac in 1993, therefore we as the district court were the first to instigate proceedings against the entire group, and for purposes of economy, all the incidents involving that group in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija were placed under the competence of the district court of Pristina for the entire group, pursuant to the Law on Criminal Procedure which stipulates precisely that way of proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whichever court starts a case finishes it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Judge Marinkovic, this paragraph 93 of the indictment, when it says, "Beginning with mid-1996 and throughout 1997 Serbian police forces responded with forceful operations," it is not accurate?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The first police operation was in March 1998, involving the attempt to arrest Adem Jashari.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you answer this question: How many attacks, according to the indictment under tab 2, targeted the police force, and what were the consequences of these attacks?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to say, very briefly, looking at the overview that I submitted to the Trial Chamber to answer the question. The terrorist group that perpetrated attacks against police patrols committed -- mounted four attacks. In the night of the 31st of August, 1996, they attacked the police building in the Klincina village, firing a hand-held grenade from a launcher that caused a fire of the building and caused the death of policemen Borislav Kozic, Armus, Djuric, and another policeman. Page 5 of the indictment --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is the indictment that we have.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Second attack, the 3rd of August, 1996, when after midnight an attack was carried out against the police building in Orlane, involving the simultaneous firing of automatic rifles preceded by the throwing of a hand grenade. This terrorist act was committed simultaneously with attacks by other terrorist groups on the same day, targeting facilities and personnel of police force in Luzane, Krpimej, and others. The third attack was carried out also in August against the police section in Celopek village, the police building, by firing weapons at the building, by activating and throwing two hand grenades and thus jeopardising the lives of the policemen on duty Radojica Nikcevic, Radojko Arsenijevic, Sasa Radojcic, and Dejan Drljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, if the police did respond with forceful operations, as is stated in paragraph 93, there is nothing inappropriate about that response, in my view at any rate. They're entitled to respond. This part of the indictment is just setting the background to the later charges. So there is really no need to dwell on this particular paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, that's the point. There were no such police actions in mid-1996 and throughout 1997, as alleged in this paragraph. The first police action was in March 1998 when an attempt was made to arrest Adem Jashari's group. So when it says here in this paragraph "From mid-1996 and throughout 1997 the police forcefully reacted," that is simply not correct. It's not true. It is correct that that would have been legal, but they did not respond at all. There was no armed conflict between the police and the terrorists, no forceful actions whatever in 1996 and 1997. The first action was in March 1998 when an attempt was made to arrest Jashari.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no. I think this point was been ventilated sufficiently. Move on to -- move on to another area now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in addition to members of the police, were civilians and their property the target of their attacks?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The facilities where refugee families lived, starting from 1995. They attacked the refugee settlement in Junik on the 7th of May, 1995. Then in Balaboc again on the 8th of May -- on the 8th of August, 1996. Then also another refugee centre on the 2nd of September, 1995. A hand grenade was thrown. I shall slow down, yes. On the 22nd of September, 1995, when a hand grenade was thrown at the teachers' school in Pristina where refugees had been put up, displaced persons. The 11th of September, 1996, in Decani, an explosive device was placed underneath the tractor of Ismet Maljokaj who cooperated with Srbija Suma, a public-owned company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He's an Albanian?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. His tractor was destroyed and the facility involved too. Now, what else did I want to say which is important for the activity of these terrorist groups? That they operated from ambushes during the night. If up look at the overview of these attacks, they attacked during the night or in the early morning. They would throw hand grenades and run away, or they would shoot at members of the MUP and their facilities and then, again, they would run away. All these attacks were launched from ambushes, so the police could not have reacted even if they had wanted to. That is what I have to say about the cases that I investigated, and this meant that many acts committed by terrorists gangs and groups were confirmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we have the point about that now. Move on to another area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 5, number 1, terrorist attacks from the 22nd of April, 1996, when several persons were killed and some were seriously wounded. You can also see that in this particular record. Judge Marinkovic, tell us, please, in addition to this information about the attacks committed and other crimes, did you get any other information during your investigation?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A terrorist attack was launched at Cakor in Decani, a catering facility. This was on the 22nd of April, 1996, sometime in the evening around 8.30 p.m., when fire was opened from automatic rifles at the windows of the building. It was activated -- hand grenades were activated and Blagoje Okuka and Djordje Dragic and Stane Radusinovic were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not hearing any more evidence about the -- no more evidence about these terrorist attacks. We have heard enough. Move on to Racak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, previously I have to deal with some other questions before I move on to Racak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What other questions?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted us to have a look at tab 3 in the first binder of exhibits. I would like to have a look at the indictment therein. KT201 of 1993 against several persons. That is in tab 3, that indictment. Now, what is this all about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the purpose of this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The purpose is that you can see something here, for example, in relation to Judge -- to Mr. Bonomy's question to Judge Marinkovic about the crimes in tab 2 related to 1995 and 1996 and the other years. Then the next indictment dates back to 1993 in tab 3. And that also shows a series of crimes that had been committed. I wanted to ask Judge Marinkovic about the criminal charges brought here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the purpose of showing that a series of crimes had been committed? Is that in dispute?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, Mr. Robinson, I explained at the beginning: As opposed to what the indictment says about forceful police attacks starting from mid-1996 and throughout 1997, which is all incorrect, here you can see along parallel lines on the one hand how terrorist attacks were committed and how people were killed, Serbs, Albanians, others. And on the other hand, along parallel lines, how state organs reacted, how they investigated cases, how they caught the perpetrators, how investigations were carried out, as Judge Marinkovic explained, how they were tried before courts of law, and how they were ultimately convicted. So this was normal legal procedure in any state where there is rule of law. This is a picture that you should have in your mind. All of this went on this way until foreign factors instigated the KLA to escalate into an organisation launching large-scale terrorist attacks when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the tab that we just looked at, tab 2.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not allowing it. You must move on to Racak. We've had enough of this.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. The interpreters cannot hear the speaker. Yes, now we can hear him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is contained in tabs 4, 5, and 6, may I ask the witness that? Because this includes the verdicts of the district court and the Supreme Court. It is claimed here that the Albanians put up passive resistance, so I wanted --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 4 I don't have a translation for, 5 I don't have a translation for, 6 I think we do have a translation for, and can I trouble the Chamber to just help me to this extent in respect of the admission of tab 2, which I understand of course is going to be admitted, there was a discussion about the particular utility of tab 2. The accused, in dealing with it immediately on return this morning, explained his understanding of the position, which was, although expressed differently, I think to the effect that he was relying on the contents of the document for its truth, and my working assumption is that's the basis upon which it's being admitted, and I'd be simply grateful for clarification of that if I'm Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. wrong. Incidentally, I have -- in case the Chamber doesn't have the precise words that the accused used to explain his purpose in the document, he said immediately after the break that it illustrates that facts that were established and taken note of in a public record provided here as exhibits --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we'll come back to that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's move on with the evidence. Mr. Milosevic, these documents that are not translated, we will not be able to deal with them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was my understanding that tab 6 had been translated. Sixty -- out of 64 documents, nine have not been translated yet. They were all given for translation, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the Presiding Judge said to you to move to Racak right now. You can come back to tab 6 and other matters after Racak. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well. If it suits you better for me to move on to Racak immediately, that is what I will do, with pleasure. Let me just move these tabs aside, because they're just bothering me here. I need to leave this aside so I can go back to it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic -- Mrs. Marinkovic, we're going to deal with Racak now. In paragraph 66a, it says: "On the 15th of January, 1999, or around that date, in the early morning hours the forces of the FRY and Serbia attacked the village of Racak (the municipality of Stimlje). After shelling, the forces of the FRY and Serbia entered the village later in the morning and began conducting house-to-house searches. Villagers, who attempted to flee from the forces of the FRY and Serbia, were shot throughout the village. A group of approximately 25 men attempted to hide in a building, but --" I'm just reading out what it says here, what is written here, so I'm not responsible for the Serbian translation and for the case endings used here "-- but were discovered by the forces of the FRY and Serbia. They were beaten and then were removed to a nearby hill, where they were shot and killed. Altogether, the forces of the FRY and Serbia killed approximately 45 Kosovo Albanians in and around Racak." And then it says: "Those persons killed who are known by name are set forth in Schedule A, which is attached as an appendix to this indictment." Before I put a question to you, I would like to draw your attention to something. I hope you have had a look at this indictment, and that's the part where I was accused of killing, the crime of killing, and under (A) it says Racak and everything that I quoted to you in relation to Racak. This is the killing that I committed. Now, Mrs. Marinkovic, since in your capacity as investigating judge already on the 15th of January you entered Racak and spent some time in the village itself, please give us an answer or, rather, what is correct from the paragraph that I read out to you? Is anything correct? Is all of it correct? Is it partly correct? I'm not putting a leading question. Just give an answer in relation to what I quoted from this paragraph of the indictment. What is correct?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not correct that there had been shelling. It is not correct that on the hill, as it says here, 25 persons were brought out and killed. Also, this other figure that is mentioned, 45 persons killed in Racak. It is not the way it is written in this indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Is there anything that is correct in this paragraph of the indictment, because you've just mentioned all of this now. Could you read this paragraph out again. Is there anything that is correct here?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I have a look at the indictment again? May I see it once again?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: By all means. In the Serbian translation, it is page 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think it's in the binder.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not in the binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's the indictment, Kosovo indictment. Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can take my copy. Go ahead, take my copy. You can take my copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We don't, I'm afraid, have a spare B/C/S version of the indictment immediately to hand.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But could you please just give it back to me immediately afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the right-hand side, you will see this big heading. "Murder," it says, then and it says "Racak."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you're not approaching this the right way, in my view. Forget the indictment for the time being. She went to Racak. Ask her questions about what she saw there, and that way you adduce the evidence that you want, and that evidence will, if it is the evidence you want, contradict what is in the indictment. That is the way Mr. Kay would do it. That's the way it's done in my system. Don't bother about the indictment. Let her tell you what she saw at Racak. She will give evidence which will contradict the indictment about 45 Kosovo Albanians killed, and she will give her evidence which will contradict what is in paragraph 66. That's the way the evidence should be adduced.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic --

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I be allowed to comment on para 98?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's not 98, it's 66.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: A very brief comment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a paragraph numbered 98 as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: A very brief comment, and then Mr. Milosevic will ask questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 66(A), I see. It says that a group of about 25 males attempted to hide in a building but were discovered by the forces of the FRY and Serbia. They were beaten and then were removed to a nearby hill where they were shot and killed. Although the forces of the FRY and Serbia killed 45 approximately Kosovo Albanians in and around Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You can make your comments and I'll ask you the questions.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is stated here is not correct because I didn't find this in Racak when I was there. Secondly, that it says that on the 15th of January, in an incident of that kind, 45 unarmed Kosovo Albanians were killed, as it says, in the village of Racak, Stimlje municipality. That is incorrect as well, because they weren't unarmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, start from the beginning. She got some information. She went to Racak. Who was with her, what did she see there, and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the 15th of January, were you yourself in Racak?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, on the 15th of January while you were in the village of Racak itself or on a later date when you tried to make an on-the-spot investigation on the 16th and 17th, did you experience the shelling of the village of Racak?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no shelling of Racak either on the 15th or a few days after that when I tried to go in, and the last day when I did manage to enter Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the 15th of January, 1999 - we're always speaking about the events in Racak of 1999, I don't want to waste time repeating the year every time - did you on the 15th of January while you were in Racak notice on the houses or in the surroundings any destruction and damages that could indicate that there had been shelling or any artillery fire whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I noticed nothing of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the paragraph I quoted from the indictment, the forces of the FRY and Serbia are mentioned. Now, what do you understand under those terms?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The forces of Serbia and the FRY is -- that was the army and the police. That's my understanding. That is what I mean when I see "FRY and Serbian forces."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, in and around the village of Racak were there any -- did any units of the Yugoslav army take part in actions there?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't see any army, any soldiers anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did the army shoot at the village of Racak?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you a moment ago about the traces of shelling and you said you saw no traces of shelling. While you were in the village on the 15th of January, on the houses and the surrounding facilities, did you notice any damages which would point to any use of firearms to any great extent within the village itself?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were no damages on the houses and I went round the whole village of Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On that same day, the 15th of January, 1999, in Racak, did you happen to notice a single civilian woman or child?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. The village was completely empty. There were no women, no children, or any civilians whatsoever. Nobody at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does that indicate? What does that show?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It shows that the village had previously been liberated, that the civilians had left the village beforehand, and that members of the terrorist gang or band had come in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, how come you were in Racak on 15th of January? Why did you go there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can explain that. In the morning in the office of the district court of Pristina where the duty investigating judge was there, and that was me, I was informed by the duty service of the SUP of Pristina, and this was common practice that the person on duty should inform the duty investigating judge of any event that took place and an on-spot, on-site investigation had been conducted. So as I say, the duty officer phoned me up and told me that in Racak there had been an incident, a conflict between individuals and terrorists that they assumed that there were casualties as a result and that I should decide whether to conduct an on-site investigation, and, if so, to inform them of that. As soon as I had completed talking to the duty officer, the public prosecutor came into my office - his name was Ismet Sufta, he was a Turk by ethnicity - and he asked me straight away, he said, "Judge, have you received information about Racak?" I confirmed that I had, and I said that I had decided that an on-site investigation should be conducted. He accepted that and we agreed to go out together and investigate. I called up the duty service to tell them of our decision, saying the prosecutor and myself decided to conduct an on-site investigation and they should ensure a vehicle to take us from Pristina to Stimlje and then from Stimlje to Racak, and at the same time the duty service or person on duty should inform the authorised crime inspector and crime technician whom we needed in order to set up a team for an investigation, scene of crime investigation and carry on with our work. At the same time, I told the duty officer that he should inform the representatives of the OSCE straight away so that they should become apprised of my decision to carry out a scene of crime investigation in Racak and that they could come and be observers if they so desired, which was in keeping with the agreement reached between the FRY government and the OSCE.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What time was it that you received the call from SUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was in the morning. I think between 8.30 and 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When did you reach Racak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me tell you, by the time we set out from Pristina to Stimlje, it takes you about half an hour to 45 minutes. In Stimlje, we had to wait for the authorities, the inspector and the crime technician to come, and then we set out, I think it was between half past one and 2.00 p.m. when we started out from Stimlje towards the village of Racak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So you would reach Racak at about what time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We reached Racak, as it says in my Official Note which I compiled linked to my investigation that day, we reached Racak at about 1400 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And according to the reports that you received, the incident at Racak would have taken place when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I learnt about the incident only when -- or the details about the incident I learnt at the police station in Stimlje when I got there, and I heard from them that it had been in the hours of the morning, early hours of the morning when the incident in Racak actually took place. After midnight, at 3.00 or 4.00 a.m., in actual fact. Around about that time, between midnight and 3.00 or 4.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but that is what you should have done when I told you to start from the beginning, Mr. Milosevic; how she got the information and how they went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: According to your information, Mrs. Marinkovic, this operation, the action was it reported to the Verification Mission of the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And on what grounds do you say that?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learnt about that on the basis of information I received at the police station in Stimlje, and I also saw on the nearby hill two orange vehicles parked on the hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You saw that on the 15th of January, which is the day that the incident in Racak occurred?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when you yourself arrived in Racak, was there still any fighting going on?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we arrived in Racak, you could hear firing and shooting coming from all sides. However, it didn't reach us. The firing and the shots didn't reach us. So we were able to approach the scene where the police had located all the weapons it had found on the surrounding hills and collected up in that particular spot. And the quantity of weapons in one spot which I myself personally saw, I and the prosecutor and the other members of the scene of crime team, the ammunition was sorted according to categories, the amounts, photographs were taken of all this, and I issued orders that all these weapons should be loaded up onto a vehicle and serve as proof, material evidence and be brought in to the SUP or the police station at Urosevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, tell me what you toured first. You arrived at about 2.00 p.m., 2.00 in the afternoon. What did you go and visit first? Did anybody give you any suggestions as to what you should go and see first? You were the investigating judge, so what did you do first?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We entered the village of Racak. We passed by the mosque and reached the place where the police was or the police who was with me, and it was their duty to provide safety and security, to secure the spot. And they took me to the place where the weapons were located.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that means the first thing you saw were the weapons. Did you see anything else in addition to the weapons that was found there, and was it all a mass collected up in one place?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one place. There was a large amount of weapons, different types of weapons. Then there were hand grenades. There were boxes with large quantities of ammunition, uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any notes on the specifications for the type of weapons found, the quantity and so on, what was found on the spot?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I made up an Official Note on the 15th of January 1999, and in that Official Note I list everything that was found, all the weapons found on -- in the area, and I have a picture, a photograph to back it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do we have that Official Note in our exhibits?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Let me have a look in the tabs, what tab this is under.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me just take a look at the binder as well.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says Racak videotape CD.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll have a look. I can't find the tab now. But I'll take a look during the break and find it, not to waste time. But let's recapitulate: You first of all went to the spot where the weapons had been collected and the other equipment that you mentioned; is that right? Now, I'll find the document during the break and find the number of the tab relating to Racak and then we'll do it that way after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Tab 40. -- 45.4 says that it's a CD of bodies found Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in a mosque, KLA equipment, and documentation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But that was on the 18th of January.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: We'll come to that in due course, Mr. Kwon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, tab -- .2, the KLA weaponry found in the village Racak, 15th of January.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll come to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, just wait a while. You don't have to look for the document now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Put the question. Put the question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We established what you first saw and where you went first. What happened afterwards, after that?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, when we had made a list of everything we found and took photographs of the weapons and loaded up the weapons that we found in the area into the vehicle, the members of the police force who were with me on the scene, who were providing security, they suggested that we look around for any victims. While we were deciding what direction to take towards the hill, which is where they thought the victims were most likely to be, they opened fire on us from all sides. Shooting came at us from all sides. There was such a lot of shooting that you couldn't hear yourself think. The most important thing was to take refuge, to get into the vehicles and leave the scene in order to save our lives, all of us who were there, to go to safety. So we got into the vehicle, left the village, and managed to reach the Stimlje police station. We waited -- we were shot at all the time. We managed to reach the police station. We waited there for a while. The shooting continued. It began to grow dark, and I was advised by the police that it was very risky to try and enter the village again to continue our scene of crime investigations, so I decided to give it up for the day because it wasn't objectively possible to go back to the village and carry out an on-site investigation, so we decided to do that the next day. Otherwise, I can also tell you, I omitted to say that a moment ago, once we entered the village we did not find any Racak inhabitants there nor any other police forces except the group of policemen who were with me there to secure the scene and to provide protection to the members of our team while conducting the scene of crime investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, let's take a look at tab 45. It is 45.1. It is a videotape -- it's a CD, in actual fact, and the date is the 15th of January, 1999. You can see the police entering the village. 45.1 is the reference number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are we going to have the video?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is there a problem locating the video, or is there a problem with the video itself? Is there some technical problem?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There shouldn't be. It's the first video segment under tab 45.1.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the AV director just received the tape a few minutes ago. Now they're working on that. A small technical problem there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: They just received it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand the tape was just received and they're working on it. There's a small technical problem. So, Mr. Milosevic, move on to something else and then we can come back to that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So we are not able for the moment to see any of the videotapes. We have three of them now. I'm really surprised to hear that they were provided only now. I was certain that the tape had been provided a long time in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We can come back to the videos.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That shouldn't be a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So when we see the tapes, we will see what they show. On the 15th of January, while you were waiting in Stimlje for a while, hoping that the situation would calm down and you would be able to continue your on-site investigation, and then it grew dark and you decided to go back to Pristina for the day?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the 16th of January, did you continue the on-site investigation?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 16th of January, again accompanied by the on-site investigation team, I left Pristina, arrived at the Stimlje police station, and as agreed with the police who were to accompany me, we went to Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you eventually reach Racak?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because on the way, before we were halfway there, fire was opened at us from all directions from a variety of weapons so that the policemen who accompanied me and who were meant to secure the scene advised me it was very risky to continue our journey towards Racak because all of our lives were in danger. I took their advice and returned, so I did not manage to conduct the on-site investigation on the 16th of January either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you were shot at on your way to Racak?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What time was it, approximately? Whenever I ask about the time, I want you to give me the approximate time. Do you know from your notes or do you remember when fire was opened at you on your way to Racak?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in the morning, around noon maybe, between noon and 1.00 p.m. I cannot remember the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you were shot at. Is it approximately the same time when William Walker was in Racak?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned later that the time when William Walker was in Racak coincided with the time when we were shot at.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did you find out that when -- while you were being -- while you were under fire William Walker was in Racak?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because for security reasons it was impossible to conduct that on-site investigations, we all returned home after agreeing that we should return the next day and attempt again to carry out this investigation. That evening, I heard on TV the statement given by Walker that allegedly a massacre took place in Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you were in Racak -- since you had been in Racak the previous day, did it sound likely to you? Did it sound probable, what he said in the statement?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe it, because I had been there on the 15th. I had seen nothing of the kind. On the 16th, I tried to go to the place again, and I was under fire, while Walker had visited the village accompanied by a crew of journalists. I saw on TV a number of armed personnel, security, who were with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did anything arouse suspicion in your mind, anything in that statement made by Walker?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was suspicious immediately of the fact that Walker had entered the village with his escorts without prior agreement and notification to me and the competent authorities, because we should have, according to procedure, gone to the village again to try to find the victims and inspect the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: KVM members attended your on-site investigations on a number of occasions prior to that.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a large number of cases, I conducted on-site investigations when OSCE representatives had already arrived at the scene in Kosovo and Metohija, and according to the agreement I mentioned earlier between the government of Yugoslavia and OSCE done in October 1998, OSCE representatives were always notified by the duty service of the SUP whenever an incident had occurred, and it was common practice that the team on duty should go out into the field. And in a number of cases, when I arrived at the scene they were already there, and they attended as observers, keeping their own notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So as investigating judge, you were well-informed about the role of this Verification Mission. You maintained cooperation with them, they attended your on-site investigations. Did OSCE representatives have the mandate to make conclusions about incidents and investigations in which no result was available immediately?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not authorised to make conclusions. It was contrary to the agreement. They had a certain mandate which authorised them to follow procedures and investigations, to monitor, to follow the movement of various units and make records if incidents occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In this particular case, you came under fire which made it impossible for you to enter Racak and conduct an on-site investigation. In your stead, Walker did an on-site investigation and informed the public about his findings. Had that happened ever before in your practice, that you were unable to conduct an on-site investigation, the Verification Mission did it in your stead?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This never happened before and that was an additional factor which made me suspicious that there was something wrong and that I as investigating judge was impeded from reaching the scene and doing the investigation myself. I thought I was being prevented from seeing something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In those many cases where KVM representatives attended your on-site investigations, did you personally invite them to attend?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was common practice, and that was our agreement, that the duty service of the SUP of Urosevac or any other town should inform the investigating judge and the public prosecutor about whatever incident had occurred, and whenever the investigating judge decided to go out on to the scene, they immediately reported it to the OSCE representatives. Thus it was not unusual for them to arrive on the scene even before I did. However, in those cases the police was already there and they did not interfere. They waited for the official on-site investigation team to arrive and then we would proceed with our cooperation. We had informal conversations. They would ask me what had happened, and we normally communicated and cooperated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's time for the break. We'll adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson. In the meantime, I have found this report related to the visit of Mrs. Marinkovic to the village of Racak on the 15th of January. It has already been exhibited. It was exhibited during the testimony of General Drewienkiewicz, and it is marked D3. I just wish to discuss it briefly. It's an Official Note that has been translated into English. It says on the 15th of January, 1999, and so on and so forth. We see in paragraph number 3 "When we arrived in Racak village, we stopped close to the mosque around 1400 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is the time you mentioned, Witness. Please may I draw your attention to this passage since I had asked you a question about weapons. Is this the report you made, because you are testifying about it today: "At the spot where we arrived in Racak, I was informed by the police," and so on, "weapons, and military uniforms. I was informed by the police that they had collected it all." What was photographed on that spot? On that day, the following weapons were found. Follows an enumeration: 12.7-millimetre Browning, 7.9-millimetre Brownings with reinforced charged --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we have that document with us, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope you do. If not, I can give you this translation into English which I have with Exhibit D3. It has already been exhibited. I'm now using it to put my questions to the witness. You can take my copy. I would ask the usher to be so kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Put it on the ELMO and indicate the part so we can follow.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the fifth paragraph, the fifth paragraph. Yes, one, two, three four, fifth passage in English. "The following weapons were found --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's page 2 in the English, the middle. Right in the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "... two mounted 7.9-millimetre Brownings with charges, 36 7.62-millimetre automatic rifles, two sniper rifles, five Chinese-made hand-held grenade launchers, two [as interpreted] Hand grenades and charges for hand-held grenade launchers, 22 hand grenades, ammunition of various calibres in the amount of 7.282 pieces -- 7.282 pieces, three portable radio transmitters, medical supplies, and military uniforms with KLA insignia." This -- these are the weapons found on the 15th. That is what you managed to establish on the 15th. The rest of the text refers to your later investigation when you continued it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will now ask the AV booth to play tab 45.1, the first video segment relating to the 15th of January. That is the clip showing the police entering the village.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There should be sound as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There is no sound at the moment, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no explanation. This footage does have sound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If there were sound, what would we be hearing?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know by heart, but there is the sound of the police entering the village. You see what's going on. You can see orange jeeps on the hill. This is not -- the visibility is not very good. I remember seeing very clearly the jeeps of the Verification Mission. We had this footage played during the testimony of General Drewienkiewicz, and the orange jeeps were clearly visible. Now we have tab 45.2 showing the weapons that were enumerated in the report of Mrs. Marinkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, you had occasion to see this videotape showing the police entering the village?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see in that videotape the orange jeeps of the Verification Mission?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw them on the hill from which spot they could observe unhampered the entry of the police into the village and what was going on in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you able to recognise Racak and the surroundings in this video footage? You watched this tape during preparation, during proofing.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You cannot see it very clearly at this moment, but you could see normally on the footage the panorama of the area of Racak, what I saw on the 15th and the 16th of January. I recognise Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does this video segment show the entry of the police into the village and the presence of two orange jeeps of the Verification Mission on the hill overlooking the village?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This second video segment that we saw, showing a cache of ammunition and military equipment that you reflected in your report, is that what you saw?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those are the same things that I saw on site. It's just like it happened yesterday, despite the many years that passed since.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was it around that time when you were already on the spot where the ammunition was that fire was opened upon you and you withdrew?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Just as we finished inventorying the weapons and ammunition, fire was opened at us from automatic weapons, incessant automatic fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that what we can see in 45.3? It doesn't seem to be in good order now, but the contributions have been provided. We can see it now on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, these videos coming without soundtrack makes it very difficult to know very much about them; for example, who they were made by, for what purpose, or what they're purporting to show. I know we had a problem yesterday, or was it the day before, last week, with a video that had to be replayed when the soundtrack had been made available, and I would ask that before we lose sight or memory of this part of the evidence, that we have it played with sound, if it's available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take that into account.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I kindly ask the technical people to play all the video clips they have, because it seems that there is something wrong with the procedure of playing the tapes. I don't understand where the problem is, because I viewed this entire Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. footage and it was fine then.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move on. The next clip where Judge Marinkovic can be seen. The next one, number 3. All of this was number 2.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the next one. Now, we're going to look at this one later. This is you; is that right? Can you please stop here and then we'll continue from there on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before you continue, Mr. Milosevic, tell us who made these tapes. How were they made?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the information I have, the first clip that shows the entry of the police where the two orange vehicles of the Verification Mission can be seen and when the police are entering Racak on the 15th, that was made a Reuters journalist who was with the police at the time, and he was present when the police entered Racak. The next one, the one with the weapons and the one after that were filmed by the journalists of Radio Television Pristina who were accompanying Judge Marinkovic while she was carrying out her investigation. Could the witness please correct me if I made a mistake or if she knows more about this, but I think that that is the point as far as the origin of this video footage is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any more precise information about this, Mrs. Marinkovic?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Professor Dobricanin and I, on the third day, the 17th, entered the village and when they shot at us and when we were hiding behind the vehicles, this was a TV crew from TV Pristina who was accompanying us. And later on, as we were touring Racak and as we entered the mosques, this official and there were so many foreign journalists present and everybody was filming this. And also there was a crime technician who was in charge of filming this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, when you say "this," what are you referring to? Are you referring to the footage with the weapons?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who did this?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The crime technician of Krusevac who was in charge of filming all of this on site. And the second clip on the 18th of January, 1999, the little bit you saw from the trenches, this was also the crime technician, that is to say an official person, part of the official team, a member of the official team who was in charge of filming with camera everything that was going on during the investigation, the on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So on number 1, you have the entrance of the -- the entry of the verifiers; and number 2 the weapons, the seizing of the weapons; and number 3 is your presence in Racak when you were being shot at. And you said that you and Dr. Dobricanin were hiding behind the car and when you were squatting there as you were being shot at?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We've just started viewing clip number 4, but before we move on, let us go back to your Official Note, the one that we had on the ELMO a few minutes ago. You explained that on the 16th you could not get into Racak because fire was opened at you. On the 16th Walker was there and he made those statements of his. And in the next paragraph of this Official Note, you say that on the 17th of January at 11.00 the investigation continued with the same team. And in the second paragraph all the persons present are enumerated.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters please have the document on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the document be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the same document that we saw a few moments ago. You had it on the ELMO a few moments ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's the Prosecution Exhibit? D3. D3.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is D3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the 17th, "The investigation resumed at 11.00 the next day with the same people participating. On the 17th of January, 1999, before going out into the field and informing OSCE representatives, I talked to the deputy chief of the Kosovo Verification Mission, British General John Drewienkiewicz. He wanted me and Dr. Sasa Dobricanin, a forensic expert from the Institute for Forensic Medicine in Pristina, to go alone, saying that they would guard us while we were conducting the investigation." I don't have the first name of Dr. Dobricanin. It's barely legible. You explained why you couldn't do anything on the 16th. Walker was in Racak, you were on the road, and on the 17th you continued your investigation.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is mentioned here that Drewienkiewicz suggested to you that you go with them. What was that all about?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the day when, as agreed, we met at the police station in Stimlje, Mr. Drewienkiewicz came with his co-workers. After the introductions, he spoke to me as if he were issuing an order to me and in a raised tone of voice, and he said what I mentioned the Official Note, that I should come with him and that Professor Dobricanin could come with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was your answer to him?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I was surprised that he was addressing me that way, as a woman and as a judge. And I tried to explain to him that according to the law, I am the only person authorised to conduct an investigation as investigating judge, and that he can come with us, he can attend as an observer, in view of the agreement, in terms of what the OSCE representatives could do. However, he did not accept my conditions, and again he continued in an angry tone of voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand you well. What were your conditions? What do you mean by "conditions"? What conditions? Did you put any conditions to him?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It wasn't me. According to the law, I am the only person authorised as an investigating judge to carry out an on-site investigation together with the other members of the team. That is what I said to him. However, he did not accept that, and he wanted me to do what he had asked me to do. When I told him that I would carry out the investigation, because according to the law I was authorised to do that, either in his presence or in his absence, and if security conditions allow we are going to go out on site together with the entire team, the investigation team, he threatened me then, and he said that he would complain to me about the -- to The Hague Tribunal. And I was really surprised that a diplomat could treat me that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not understanding what it was he said to you that was unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was unacceptable was that he asked me to go alone with him to carry out the investigation, without the other members of the team and without the police who are in charge of providing security on site. Of course I did not accept that. First of all, because before that, two days before that we were shot at.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "team," in the second paragraph of this Official Note, which I did not quote but now that has become a topical issue as well through this question, you said the team for on-site investigations consisting of the following, the deputy municipal prosecutor Ismet Sufta, the inspector from the SUP Urosevac Dabic Dragan and Bozinic Sasa, along with a group of police from the police station at Stimlje. We set out to the site. So with the same team, the same people, you intended to carry out the investigation. Is that the customary composition of such teams; the prosecutor, the SUP inspector, and the crime technician?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the way it is according to law and that is the customary practice, that members of the team are the persons mentioned here. Of course. Not by name and surname but in terms of their official capacity. However on the 17th I also asked an expert to come along, Professor Dr. Slavisa Dobricanin so that he, as a pathologist, as a forensic expert, be present as well in case we find victims in Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, in relation to your conversation with General John Drewienkiewicz, in the last paragraph on page 1 of your statement, that is the first -- of your report, rather, and that is the first -- that is the first paragraph on page 3 in the English translation, so could you please find that. "When I explained to him how an investigation is carried out and that "--

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot follow this. We're sorry. It's very fast and we don't have the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about page 2, last paragraph. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It has to do with what the witness explained a few minutes ago. "He said he wanted me to go alone accompanying him, together with a forensic expert, Dr. Sasa Dobricanin..." However, I already quoted that passage. Very well. It's at the end of the page in Serbian. "When I explained to him how and in which way investigations are carried out --" and so on and so forth. "He then wanted the police to go without uniforms and weapons as otherwise there might be a conflict in the village of Racak. He explained that the villagers had weapons and that they might open fire if they saw police in uniform. Since I did not accept this, saying that the investigation team were going out into the field and that they could come along to monitor our work, he openly threatened me, saying that he would do his best to have me brought before The Hague Tribunal and that he would appear as a witness because I was to blame for the 'bloodbath' which had happened and which would happen if I went to the site that day in the presence of the police."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the question, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what was your answer to him in response to that, Mrs. Marinkovic?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what? I was really surprised. First he said that there were unarmed villagers in the village. And after that, when he was in such a rage, he did not refer to unarmed villagers again when I said that the police were coming along with us in order to provide security. Then in this rage he said that the villagers were armed and that they would use the arms to shoot at the police. So I did not understand what this was all about. Were they armed or were they unarmed? And for two days already those villagers were shooting at us and were not permitting us to carry out the on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, Mrs. Marinkovic, Richard Ciaglinski, on the 16th of April, 2002 here, when he testified, said, and I'm going to quote a portion of what he said, and this is what he said: He said that General DZ - Drewienkiewicz - on several occasions emphasised to Judge Marinkovic that if anything happened to our verifiers because of her unthought-out acts, that he would definitely report her name to The Hague Tribunal as an individual who had committed a war crime by unnecessarily bringing the lives of the verifiers into danger. So he confirms what you said.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But what were the reasons he gave? Why were you threatening -- bringing the lives of the verifiers in danger if you conducted the investigation?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He never mentioned this. I hear this for the first time today, that in the village of Racak the verifiers were present. There was no discussion of that at all, nor did I know that there were any verifiers in the village of Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Then he said -- then he told you that the villagers were armed. Well, did you ask him how come they were armed if they were unarmed before that?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I asked him that, he couldn't give me an answer because he contradicted himself. First of all he said they were unarmed and then he said they were armed and that they -- the villagers would open fire on the police force. So he didn't have an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did he try to intervene with the Yugoslav authorities, prevail there in respect of what was going on?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said that I would go to the on-site investigation with or without him, the important thing was that I had decided to conduct an investigation if the circumstances permitted. He asked who my boss was in Belgrade, for me to give him his name so that he could inform his boss, Walker, that that boss of mine in Belgrade should prevail upon me and prevent me from going to the scene of the crime. And I said that I have no boss, that I myself am my own boss when it comes to this investigation and the investigative process and that at that point in time I was head of the parade and that I would decide what steps would be taken in the investigation, and secondly, what was to be established on the scene of the crime in the village of Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And pursuant to our provisions, can anybody issue orders to the investigating judge with respect to an investigation?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The investigating judge is independent and autonomous, and it is up to him to make the decision, to decide what steps he's going to take in the investigation if he considers the steps to be relevant and what steps he considers to be relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. John Drewienkiewicz on the 11th of April, 2002, claimed here that you personally had asked for larger police forces to enter Racak for your own safety and security. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not true. The number -- we didn't discuss the police at all or the number of policemen. We discussed -- what we discussed was that Drewienkiewicz wanted to prevent me from carrying out the on-site investigation in the village of Racak and I wanted to proceed. So that was the only clash between the two of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said, though, there was no mention of police. Drewienkiewicz said that on that occasion he told you that a large presence of policemen in Racak would be more of a provocation than anything else; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't mention the police. I didn't bring the police up at all. That was his opinion. I don't know on what assumptions he based his opinion, but we know that it is quite normal and natural and pursuant to the law that the police, together with the investigating team, goes out to the scene of the crime, and the police is there to secure the area so that the investigating judge can conduct his investigation unimpeded. Now, how many policemen isn't up to me. That is decided by the police force itself. The police force assesses the security situation and decides how many policemen it's going to send out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Drewienkiewicz also said, and he was referring to the OSCE, that they were there to guarantee your security. Did he tell you that?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he told me that but I asked him how could the verifiers provide security and guarantee our security and escort us when we know that the verifiers were unarmed? They did not carry weapons on them, as was provided for by the agreement between the federal government and the OSCE representatives. And so the OSCE representatives were provided security by our state organs, in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did Drewienkiewicz in Racak have his men, as he claimed in his statement here on the 11th of April and that he needed time to withdraw those men?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't mention that to me. I didn't know about that. He didn't bring that up again at all during the conversation we had. I didn't know about it nor did he tell me that he had his verifiers or associates in the village.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic and Mrs. Marinkovic, the interpreters are asking you to speak more slowly. Please observe a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Marinkovic, Drewienkiewicz said here that when you entered the village with the investigating team, that there was an exchange of fire that took place. Is that true and correct?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not true. On the 17th of January, we attempted to enter the village of Racak but we were prevented from doing so once again because they opened fire on us once again, as you can see on the footage where I and Professor Dobricanin are seeking refuge. So we didn't manage to enter the village of Racak. We had to go back. Otherwise our lives would have been in jeopardy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the point of my question was whether there was an exchange of gunfire, as he stated here, that when you entered there was an exchange of gunfire. We saw you hiding behind a car. Was there an exchange of gunfire?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no exchange of gunfire, no. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we saw that there was -- they were shooting at you.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were shooting at us from all sides, and the only vehicle to protect us at that point was that vehicle. We hid behind it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, did our police respond to the gunfire? Did our police open fire and respond?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day it did not. There were not many policemen. They did their best to protect us and defend us. However, there was shooting coming from the surrounding hills from all sides. It was a burst of gunfire all around us and the police shot, but they didn't know which direction to shoot at and target because there was fire coming at us from all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now to speed up this process, on the next day, the 18th, did you manage to enter Racak and complete your investigation?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 18th of January, we did manage to enter the village of Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now see the rest of tab 45, that is to say the rest of tape 4 where we can see Mrs. Marinkovic and the mosque. And I think you can see Professor Dobricanin as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "Over 90 minutes. I offered to help the judge [inaudible] "We couldn't hear you, sir. Can you say that again? "For other 90 minutes I offered to help the judge to move her party to Racak in order to carry out the investigation provided there were no armed policemen with the -- [inaudible]"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This should be tab -- they started playing the tab before, and it should be the continuation. We have it, the 18th of January.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we speed this up so we can see the trenches and all the other things that were filmed later on, the footage to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, this is the footage made by -- filmed by your crime technician?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The comments being made here refers to the files or lists. He's asking for translation on the spot.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the photographs that were found.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "A list of KLA members should be given under numbers."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor Dobricanin can be heard there speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can we see -- or, rather, we can see the on-site investigation being conducted. Weapons again.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
